description: Close gravitational encounters require smaller timesteps for accuracy, while distant particles can use larger steps. Adaptive timestepping adjusts dt based on local dynamics — either globally (shortest timescale dominates) or per-particle (block timesteps). The IAS15 integrator achieves machine-precision accuracy by adaptively choosing timesteps using a 15th-order Gauss-Radau quadrature.
mathematical_formalization: Timestep criterion: dt_i = eta * min(|v_i / a_i|, sqrt(|r_ij_min| / |a_i|)). Block timestepping: round dt_i down to nearest power of 2 fraction of the global step. Particles on shorter timesteps are integrated more frequently. Error estimator for adaptive control: err = |x_full - x_half| / tol, where x_half uses two half-steps.
analogical_connections: Adaptive mesh refinement in CFD: refine spatial resolution where gradients are steep, just as adaptive timesteps refine temporal resolution where forces change rapidly
TCP congestion control: adjusts packet rate based on network conditions, analogous to adjusting dt based on dynamical conditions
Attention mechanisms in transformers: allocate more compute to important tokens, like allocating more timesteps to close encounters
implementation_hypothesis: Start with global adaptive: estimate error by comparing full-step and two half-step results. If error > tolerance, halve dt; if error < tolerance/10, double dt. For a minimal sim, this is sufficient. Advanced: implement power-of-2 block timesteps for per-particle adaptation.
experiment_seed: Simulate a highly eccentric binary orbit (e=0.99). Compare fixed timestep (tuned to perihelion) vs global adaptive vs block timestep. Measure: total force evaluations, energy conservation, wall-clock time. Adaptive should use 10-100x fewer evaluations.
